title: We Were Unable to Report on the Role of the ECB: What the Auditors Found and What They Were Refused
participants: Private holders of Greek government bonds

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The headline numbers are the auditors': "Funding for the first programme (GLF), in 2010, was 110 billion euros; for the second (EFSF; 2012) it was 172.6 billion euros and for the third (ESM; 2015) it was 86 billion euros." Of the second, "The Euro area countries finally contributed 141.8 billion euros in the form of loans from the European Financial Stability Facility (EFSF) that had been created for this purpose" — a facility built to make the loan it then made.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was procedural and the audit is blunt about it: "At the start of the Greek programme, the Commission had no experience in the management of such a process. Procedures were established after almost a year", and "There were no specific internal Commission guidelines on the actual design of the programmes' conditions, for example in terms of scope or level of detail." Conditions covering "virtually all the functions of the Greek state" were written without guidelines on how to write them.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog is institutional and the auditors name it as a refusal rather than an obscurity: "Despite the complex institutional arrangements within the programmes, the operational details of the Commission's co-operation with programmes partners, primarily the IMF and the ECB, were never formalised." And then the harder finding: the Court attempted to examine the ECB's involvement, "However, the ECB questioned the Court's mandate in this respect; did not provide sufficient amount of evidence and thus we were unable to report on the role of the ECB in the Greek programmes." One of the three parties to the arrangement is simply absent from the audit of it, at its own insistence.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The money that is traceable went into the banks. The financial sector was "substantially re-structured, but this came at a cost of over 45 billion euros injected into the banking system, out of which only a small part can potentially be recovered." The 2012 restructuring "affecting about 206 billion euros of Greek government bonds" produced "a 37.7 billion euros loss for all Greek banks, wiping out their entire capital base", after which "the four larger banks had to be recapitalised by 28.6 billion euros".
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: There was no evaluation to bury, because there was no evaluation: "The Commission did not carry out a comprehensive evaluation of the first two programmes, although such an analysis could be pertinent for adjusting the reform process." Two programmes and roughly €280 billion of commitments were succeeded by a third without a comprehensive review of either.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Greek euro membership and the borrowing it permitted — "From the time of its entry into the euro, Greece benefitted from an economic boom fuelled by easy access to borrowing and generous fiscal policy" — together with "revelations about misreporting of official statistics" that destroyed confidence in the numbers.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: Two permanent lending institutions created to fund the programmes, the EFSF for the second and the ESM for the third, and a conditionality practice reaching "virtually all the functions of the Greek state" — built, as the audit says, without guidelines.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Official loans finance the sovereign; the sovereign's restructuring destroys the capital of the banks that hold its bonds; recapitalising those banks is financed by further official loans to the sovereign; the sovereign's debt ratio rises. The auditors record the result arithmetically: "In 2016, public debt in Greece exceeded 181 % of GDP compared to 126.7 % in 2009."

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the Greek bailouts were never about Greece — that the 2010 programme existed to buy time for French and German banks to unload their Greek bonds before the 2012 write-down, so that the losses landed on European taxpayers and Greek pensioners instead of the banks that had lent recklessly.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: THIS AUDIT CANNOT SETTLE IT, AND SAYING SO IS THE POINT OF CITING IT. Special Report 17/2017 is an audit of the European Commission's MANAGEMENT of the programmes. It does not analyse who held Greek sovereign debt in 2010, does not track any foreign bank's exposure over the following two years, and names no bank. Anyone who cites it for the de-risking claim is citing it for something it does not contain, and this dossier does not. Two things in it do bear on the claim, in opposite directions. Against the strongest form of the decoy: private holders were not spared. "Private investors were asked to agree to write off 53.5 % of the face value of their Greek government bonds", contributing "approximately 107 billion euros", across "about 206 billion euros of Greek government bonds" — a write-down of that size is not what a successful escape looks like. For the decoy's underlying worry: the losses that followed were socialised, and the auditors quantify them — €37.7 billion wiped out the entire capital base of the Greek banks, €28.6 billion recapitalised the four largest, and over €45 billion went into the banking system of which "only a small part can potentially be recovered". The timing question — whether exposure had already moved before the write-down, and to whom — remains open on this record. AND THE AUDIT RECORDS ITS OWN BLIND SPOT, which is the most useful thing in it: the European Court of Auditors tried to examine the ECB's role and was refused. "The ECB questioned the Court's mandate in this respect; did not provide sufficient amount of evidence and thus we were unable to report on the role of the ECB in the Greek programmes." A third of the Troika is missing from the official audit because it declined to be audited.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: European Court of Auditors Special Report No 17/2017, "The Commission's intervention in the Greek financial crisis", issued under Article 287(4) TFEU. It records: programme funding of €110 billion (GLF, 2010), €172.6 billion (EFSF, 2012, of which euro area countries finally contributed €141.8 billion) and €86 billion (ESM, 2015); objectives met "only to a limited extent", with GDP shrinking "by over a quarter", no return to growth in 2012 as envisaged, a debt-to-GDP ratio that "kept increasing" despite large-scale fiscal consolidation, and short-term financial stability achieved without averting a sharp deterioration in bank balance sheets; public debt exceeding 181% of GDP in 2016 against 126.7% in 2009; no Commission experience at the outset, procedures established after almost a year, no internal guidelines on designing conditions, inadequate prioritisation in the first two programmes and no embedding in a broader country strategy; cooperation with the IMF and ECB never formalised; the Private Sector Involvement write-off of 53.5% of face value contributing approximately €107 billion across about €206 billion of bonds, causing a €37.7 billion loss that wiped out the Greek banks' entire capital base and required €28.6 billion of recapitalisation for the four largest, with over €45 billion injected into the banking system of which only a small part may be recovered; no comprehensive evaluation of the first two programmes; and the Court's express inability to report on the ECB's role because the ECB questioned its mandate and did not provide sufficient evidence.

citations.title: European Court of Auditors, Special Report No 17/2017, "The Commission's intervention in the Greek financial crisis" (pursuant to Article 287(4), second subparagraph, TFEU)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from the European Court of Auditors (2.3 MB) and read as extracted text; the executive summary and the conclusions were read in full and the body selectively. THE PROGRAMMES, AS THE AUDITORS SIZE THEM: "Funding for the first programme (GLF), in 2010, was 110 billion euros; for the second (EFSF; 2012) it was 172.6 billion euros and for the third (ESM; 2015) it was 86 billion euros." "The Euro area countries finally contributed 141.8 billion euros in the form of loans from the European Financial Stability Facility (EFSF) that had been created for this purpose." THE VERDICT: "As of mid-2017, Greece still requires external financial support and we found that the objectives of the programmes were met only to a limited extent." On each stated objective: "Return to growth: GDP shrank during the programmes by over a quarter and Greece did not return to growth, as initially envisaged, in 2012." "Fiscal sustainability: there was large scale fiscal consolidation in terms of structural balances. But due to adverse macroeconomic developments and interest costs on existing debt, the debt to GDP ratio kept increasing." "Financial stability: the programmes ensured short-term financial stability, but were unable to avert a sharp deterioration of the banks' balance sheets". And the arithmetic: "In 2016, public debt in Greece exceeded 181 % of GDP compared to 126.7 % in 2009". ON HOW THE PROGRAMMES WERE RUN: "At the start of the Greek programme, the Commission had no experience in the management of such a process. Procedures were established after almost a year"; "There were no specific internal Commission guidelines on the actual design of the programmes' conditions"; the first two programmes "did not adequately prioritise their relative importance and they were not embedded in a broader strategy for the country"; and "Despite the complex institutional arrangements within the programmes, the operational details of the Commission's co-operation with programmes partners, primarily the IMF and the ECB, were never formalised." Also: "The Commission did not carry out a comprehensive evaluation of the first two programmes". THE PART WHERE THE AUDITOR IS REFUSED, which is a documented event and not an inference: "In line with the ECA's mandate to audit the operational efficiency of the management of the ECB, we have attempted to examine the Bank's involvement in the Greek Economic Adjustment Programmes. However, the ECB questioned the Court's mandate in this respect; did not provide sufficient amount of evidence and thus we were unable to report on the role of the ECB in the Greek programmes." WHO TOOK LOSSES, AS THE REPORT RECORDS IT: "A key element of the second programme was the Private Sector Involvement (PSI), under which private investors contributed approximately 107 billion euros by writing down part of the value of their debt holdings" — "private investors were asked to agree to write off 53.5 % of the face value of their Greek government bonds". The restructuring affected "about 206 billion euros of Greek government bonds" and "resulted in a 37.7 billion euros loss for all Greek banks, wiping out their entire capital base", after which "the four larger banks had to be recapitalised by 28.6 billion euros". Across the programmes the financial sector restructuring "came at a cost of over 45 billion euros injected into the banking system, out of which only a small part can potentially be recovered". WHAT THIS AUDIT DOES NOT EXAMINE, AND SO CANNOT SUPPORT: it is an audit of the European Commission's management. It does not analyse the nationality or identity of the bondholders repaid between 2010 and 2012, does not track changes in any foreign bank's Greek exposure over that period, and names no bank. Any claim that the first programme's purpose or effect was to let French and German banks exit before the write-down is outside what was read here and is not asserted by this dossier.
